title: TA8-02285
frame:
Forum: Refugee Protection Division (first-instance tribunal).
Parties: the claimant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review: none; this is the first-instance decision.
How the layers nest here: The member of the tribunal is the author (layer 1). The claimant and the Minister make submissions to the member (layer 2). There is no earlier decision-maker unless the reasons describe a prior decision (layer 3). Testimony and documents are layer 5.

paragraphs.text: XXXX XXXXX, a citizen of Moldova, claims refugee protection pursuant to Sections 96 and 97(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA). 1 ALLEGATIONS
The full basis for the refugee claim is set out in the narrative of the claimant's Personal Information Form2 (PIF). The following is a summary.

The claimant claims protection based on a well-founded fear of persecution for reasons of his sexual orientation; a bisexual. He was born in XXXXX, 100 km. from XXXXX. He claims he was subjected to harassment, intimidation and threats by students in XXXXX while attending the Moldovan XXXXX XXXXX from XXXXX 2000 to XXXX 2004 where he received a diploma in XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX 2004.3 He alleged he was beaten by homophobic co-workers and neighbours in XXXX 2004, XXXX 20074 and XXXXX 20075 and forced to resign from his job in XXXX 2006 and XXXXX 2007. He talked to police three times; an officer was called to the hospital in XXXX 2004 and XXXX 2007 in XXXXX and in XXXXX in XXXXX 2007. The police did not conduct sufficient investigations or provide adequate state protection. He and his friend XXXX decided to leave Moldova and they paid a company to obtain fraudulent passports for them. XXXX was returned to Moldova when his false passport was detected by the Ukrainian authorities. As a result, the claimant who had passed through customs before XXXXX continued his travels and he arrived in Canada on XXXXX 2007. His claim for protection was made on 7 January 2008. He fears harm or death if returned to Moldova.

I find that the claimant is not a Convention refugee as he does not have a well-founded fear of persecution for a Convention ground in Moldova. I also find the claimant is not a person in need of protection in that his removal to Moldova would not subject him personally to a risk to his life or to a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment. Procedural Matters

On 17 June 2010 the claimant's hearing was adjourned for lack of time. Counsel had not yet questioned the claimant. The hearing scheduled to resume on 30 September 2010 was postponed until 2 March 2011 due to counsel's unavailability. On 2 March 2011 the RPD and claimant were advised in writing and by phone that counsel was unable to attend due to XXXXX. On 2 March the claimant told the Presiding Member he wished to proceed without counsel to bring the hearing to a conclusion. After some questions and discussion about the claimant's options the Member granted a recess to allow the claimant an opportunity to further confer with his friends who had accompanied him to the hearing for moral support. After the recess the claimant again advised the Member he wished to proceed rather than postpone. The Member was satisfied this was an informed decision made by the claimant and the hearing proceeded without counsel. The two friends remained in the room for a period of time as observers.6 After a few questions in the presence of the observers, the Member noted that the claimant seemed uncomfortable answering questions about his relationships and with the agreement of the claimant the Member asked the observers to leave the room. ANALYSIS Identity

The claimant's identity as a citizen of Moldova is established by the oral testimony and the personal documents filed, including his birth certificate7 and his Moldovan photo identity card.8 Credibility

There is an issue of credibility in this claim. There is a presumption that a witness is telling the truth unless there is valid reason to doubt their truthfulness.9 There were inconsistencies and omission with regard to central aspects of his claim and failure to produce some documentary corroboration that might reasonably be available to him. The determinative issue is whether it is credible that the claimant was targeted by homophobes based on his bisexual/homosexual relationship. The panel finds that the claimant lacked credibility and as such, the claimant has not established a well-founded fear of persecution, based on membership in a particular social group. The claimant's account of the attacks he suffered as a bisexual man lacked credibility.

The claimant described an attack in XXXXX in XXXX 2004 immediately after his graduation ceremony that lacked credibility and consistency with the PIF. Many details he provided at the hearing were omitted from the PIF. In the PIF he noted he was "attacked and beaten up by a group of homophobic males". At the hearing he added salient details about the attackers, including names of two of the attackers he identified as fellow classmates. He said after he was approached by XXXXX and XXXXX and two others they began to insult and then hit him causing him to fall to the ground where he was kicked before they walked away. He said he recognized two of the attackers from one of his classes. The claimant said he was unable to get up off the ground and an ambulance came and the doctor who examined him told him there were no serious injuries. He does not know who called the ambulance. He said he spent a couple of hours at the hospital, no treatment was provided, he was not admitted to the hospital but a police officer attended at the hospital to ask what happened and the officer took the claimant's information. The claimant did not tell the officer it was a homophobic attack. He never followed up with the police about their investigation. The claimant said he did not know whether anyone witnessed the attack. The claimant speculated that the police conducted an investigation but he did not know what the police did with the information. He also said he thought the police did little after they learned he was gay. The claimant was not clear about what he meant by this. He did not know whether the police were told homophobia was the motive for the attack. He did not tell the police it was because of his sexuality. The claimant never spoke with the police again about this beating explaining that he thought it was not safe for him to ask the police anything. He speculated that the police had done nothing because he was never called regarding a subsequent proceeding. There were no documents provided to the RPD to support his claims about this attack, the doctor's exam or the police report. In contrast to his oral evidence that there were no serious injuries only bruises and no treatment provided, in the PIF narrative he stated that he required medical treatment. In contrast to telling the Tribunal Officer that he did not tell the police it was a homophobic attack and he did not know whether anybody saw the attack the claimant in his PIF stated the police did nothing when they understood the motive. He did not explain on what he based his speculation about the police knowledge of the motive. The claimant did not explain the inconsistencies between the oral evidence and PIF narrative.

He indicated that his parents were made aware of his sexuality as a result of this attack in XXXX 2004. He suspects the Dean told them. At the second sitting he contradicted this information and said that it was in 2007 that his family became aware of his sexuality. His explanation for the inconsistency was that they were previously in denial.

The claimant did not provide the RPD with medical or other supporting documents regarding the alleged incidents that occurred near the university building in 2004. His explanation for the absence of a record of treatment in his medical book was because his permanent registration is in XXXXX and his XXXXX propiska was temporary. The claimant lived in XXXXX from 2000 to 2007. At the hearing he said he did not know where the medical treatment he received while in XXXXX got recorded. I do not find that this explanation by the claimant has satisfactorily explained the absence of documents in 2004 because of the temporary status of his XXXXX propiska given he provided a medical certificate10 from XXXXX regarding a dislocated shoulder in XXXX 2007. I do not accept on a balance of probabilities that he would have no record of the 2004 doctor examination for the reason he provided about being registered in XXXXX. I find his inability to provide a satisfactory explanation for the absence of documents relating to the 2004 attack undermines his credibility. While he claims the dislocated shoulder was the result of a homophobic attack there is nothing indicated in the medical report11 about the circumstances of his injury.

At the hearings, the claimant claims he was forced to resign from employment in 2006 and 2007 because of his sexual orientation. The evidence regarding his employment was found to be inconsistent and there were further omissions between the PIF and oral evidence. In his PIF narrative he indicated he was forced to resign in XXXX 2006 but there is nothing in the PIF that this happened in XXXXX 2007. In his PIF narrative before he states "we were forced to resign in XXXX 2006", he stated co-workers and neighbours became suspicious of them as a result of XXXXX's indiscreet language and their raised voices. In the work book provided to the RPD it states "ceased employment.12 At the hearing, when asked to explain why he left the job he had held for two years his first response was that he had been "laid off". He then said he left because "I wanted to leave" and finally he said he left because "they asked me to leave". At the hearing no reference was made by the claimant to his arguments with XXXXX also employed at XXXXX. His last comment in response to the question was that he was asked to leave because of his sexual orientation. I find the claimant's inconsistent and varied answers raised credibility concerns as to the real reason he left his employment at XXXXX. The employment record book indicates he "ceased employment" on XXXXX 2006. Notwithstanding the fact that the claimant was laid off or terminated or resigned on XXXXX he apparently was able to commence employment elsewhere within five days. His employment record book indicates his employment as an XXXXX at XXXXX commenced from XXXXX 2006 until XXXXX 2007.13 The claimant left Moldova in XXXXX 2007. In addition to my adverse credibility finding regarding his varied and inconsistent evidence concerning the circumstances of his departure from XXXXX, I find based on his quick employment elsewhere in XXXXX that if it concerned his sexuality the claimant was not sufficiently disadvantaged from earning a livelihood due to his sexual orientation to constitute persecution. If his employment status in XXXX 2006 changed unexpectedly as he claims I find that he did not experience difficulty in gaining employment at another company. His workbook shows he remained at the second place until he "ceased employment" on XXXXX 2007.14 The claimant graduated from University in XXXX 2006 and was steadily employed from XXXXX 2004 until XXXXX 2007. There is nothing stated in the PIF narrative about his having to resign from his job in XXXXX 2007 because of sexual orientation. The claimant did not indicate this at the hearing. At the second sitting the Member asked whether he left this position because he was preparing to leave the country and at this point he said he was laid off because of his sexuality. He told the Member that his manager asked him to write a letter to cease employment because his manager said he knew he was gay and sleeping with men and he did not want anybody like that working in his company. It was noted that in addition to omitting from the PIF he was asked to resign in 2007, all of this information was omitted from his PIF. He was given an opportunity to explain why he had omitted this from his narrative and he said that he did not know why it was not included because he told this to the person preparing his PIF. He added that he was advised he would have an opportunity to include details at the hearing. He answered in the affirmative that he told the person preparing his PIF that his manager of one and a half years said he knew he was gay and asked for a resignation letter. The claimant was asked why he signed the declaration that the PIF was complete, true and correct if this was omitted and answered it was "true and correct" but he did not know about "complete". The Federal Court stated in Basseghi: It is not incorrect to say that answers in a PIF should be brief but it is incorrect to say that the answers should not be complete with all of the relevant facts. All relevant and important facts should be included in one's PIF. The oral evidence should go on to explain the information contained in the PIF.15 I think it reasonable to have expected this important detail to be in the PIF and particularly find it so because the person preparing the PIF included the claimant's reference to a forced resignation in XXXX 2006. I draw an adverse finding as a result of the omission and the claimant's unsatisfactory explanation for the omission. Based on the evidence, I find on a balance of probabilities that it cannot be ruled out that it was by claimant's choice he ceased employment or changed jobs when he did. I find that the claimant did not provide clear, straightforward evidence about the reason he left his job at XXXXX XXXXX in XXXX 2006.16 I find he did not satisfactorily explain why he omitted from his PIF that his manager in 2007 required him to leave. Based on the evidence before me I am unable, on a balance of probabilities, to conclude that the claimant was forced to leave his job because of his sexuality.

In XXXXX 2007 he and XXXXX were allegedly beaten and verbally insulted by XXXXX's neighbours. The claimant said he suffered a shoulder injury when he put his arm out as he fell. XXXXX suffered a bloody nose, cut lip. The claimant did not know what caused the attackers to leave when they did. He claimed that after the attackers left he and XXXXX were sitting in shock on a bench for ten minutes when an ambulance pulled up and took them to the hospital. He speculated the neighbours had called for the ambulance but there was nobody around them when the ambulance arrived. The claimant did not explain why after suffering a homophobic attack neither he nor XXXXX would attempt to take cover from further attack, or leave the area, or call for help. It was unclear what they were waiting for because neither of them called the ambulance or knew one was coming. They went to the hospital and the claimant was treated for a dislocated shoulder.17 The XXXXX medical certificate does not indicate how the injury occurred. The police were not told about the verbal insults or the suspected motive for the beating. The claimant's evidence about this incident was very similar to the evidence he provided about the XXXX 2004 incident. While the claimant provided answers to questions asked he did not spontaneously provide information about what took place. I found his overall testimony and demeanour while testifying about the beatings lacked a ring of truth. He seemed reluctant in answering questions about the police reports. He did not appear to be drawing from personal experience. The claimant and XXXXX did not call the police to follow up on their investigation.

The claimant claims in XXXXX 2007 he and XXXXX were beaten outside a café in XXXXX by seven people including two former co-workers. They were told to get out of Moldova and the claimant was hit in the face by a fist and fell and hit his head. The attackers walked away after hitting the claimant and XXXXX. The claimant said he asked XXXXX to make the one hour drive to his hometown XXXXX for medical treatment because he was afraid there was no protection in XXXXX. They drove there from the scene of the attack. The claimant presented some pages of patient chart excerpts from Regional Hospital of XXXXX written in Romanian.18 Nowhere on the certified translation pages does the name of the claimant appear. At the second sitting the Member was shown an original medical book which contained his name on the front cover. The Tribunal Officer asked the claimant why he did not seek treatment outside of XXXXX but closer than XXXXX and the claimant said he did not know why. He told the officer the previous medical treatment in XXXXX was satisfactory but that the police never did anything to help them and he feared the attackers would come to the hospital looking for them. When asked if he chose to go to XXXXX for treatment because his family was there or because he wanted to leave the place of his attack he indicated the latter. He said he just wanted to be far from XXXXX. Both he and XXXXX returned to XXXXX after receiving treatment. XXXXX drove back the next day and the claimant returned after he was released from the hospital. The claimant was unable to say why he did not go to a hospital outside of XXXXX. The claimant failed to satisfactorily explain why they quickly returned to XXXXX despite him allegedly insisting that XXXXX drive one hour with a bloody nose and him vomiting from a hit to the head due to his fear of staying in XXXXX. I found the claimant's evidence in the circumstances described lacked common sense and credibility. Despite the Tribunal Officer's questions in this area the claimant failed to satisfactorily explain why he did not remain longer with his family or in his home town until they arranged to leave the country given his claim that he feared being in the hospital in XXXXX. The claimant failed to satisfactorily explain the decision to return to XXXXX notwithstanding his alleged subjective fear. The claimant said he was never attacked more than once by the same people.

It was found that elements of the material aspects of this claim for refugee protection were not supported by credible evidence. The Board has been upheld when making reasonable findings based upon implausibility, common sense and rationality and may reject evidence if it is not consistent with the probabilities affecting the case as a whole, even if that evidence is uncontradicted.19 In this case the claimant's testimony also contained inconsistencies and implausibilities. The claimant's claim lacked credibility with regard to what happened to him as a result of his homosexual relationships and implausibilities with regard to material aspects of his claim. The determinative issue in this case is whether it is credible that the claimant was targeted by homophobes based on his bisexual/homosexual relationships. The panel finds that the claimant lacked credibility and as such the claimant has not established a well-founded fear of persecution, based on membership in a particular social group. I do not believe on a balance of probabilities the experiences he alleged in Moldova for reasons of his sexual orientation. I therefore find his claim fails pursuant to Section 96 of IRPA.

The claimant submitted that he is a current member of the XXXXXXXXXXXXX in Toronto, Ontario20 and a member of the XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX held at Metropolitan XXXXXXXXXXXXX Toronto (XXXX).21 The Member noted that the person who signed the Church letter was one of the observers introduced to the Presiding Member as a "friend" of the claimant. This same person was also photographed with the claimant.22 The claimant was unable to explain why he had provided the RPD with a photo taken with this man. His response was that his counsel advised him to send photos and letters from XXX to the RPD. The claimant said he was a member of XXX Church; however the claimant was unable to answer the Member's question as to what XXX stood for. He explained he never paid attention but that it is a bisexual church. I find that membership in a community organization is not indicative of sexual orientation as anyone can join a community organization or attend an event. The membership document merely indicates that he was a member and does not indicate anything regarding the claimant's sexual orientation. It is reasonable to expect the claimant to be able to supply reasons for providing the photos he chose to send in. I find the claimant's inability to do so suggest the motive was unclear and possibly suspect. The membership information is insufficient when compared with the credibility findings based on the claimant's testimony. Therefore, on a balance of probabilities, the claimant is not a bisexual/homosexual and it is not credible that the claimant was targeted in Moldova by homophobes based on his bisexuality/homosexual relationship. While the observer and person who signed the church letter wrote that "we have no reason to doubt XXXX fears or sexual orientation", the Member who must ultimately make the credibility findings for the claimant's refugee claim does not agree.

I reached my decision after considering all of the evidence provided. Differences in the treatment of various groups exist to a greater or lesser extent in many societies. Not all persons treated differently are victims of persecution. The claimant claimed his teachers treated him differently and his marks were lowered. The claimant completed four years of University education and obtained a diploma in his specialty field of XXXXX and XXXXX XXXXX. He was employed in XXXXX and XXXXX from graduation up until he left the country.23 Based on the available evidence I do not find that the claimant has suffered a serious restriction on his right to earn his livelihood or access to normally available educational facilities.

I find that the claimant will not face a serious possibility of persecution in Moldova based on membership in a particular social group. For the same reasons, having taken into account all the evidence, I further find that the claimant's removal to Moldova, will not subject him personally to a danger, believed on substantial grounds to exist, of torture, and will not subject him personally to a risk to his life, or a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment, under Section 97(1) of the IRPA. Therefore the claimant's claim fails on all three grounds.

For all the foregoing reasons, the Refugee Protection Division determines that the claimant is not a Convention refugee and is not a person in need of protection.
